clue.text: Beautiful creation Pisan admits is leaning to one side

indicators.note: to admit is to let something in, so one word takes the other inside it

parts.note: taken as written: of Pisa
art is beautiful creation

explanation.surface: Someone admires a famous creation from Pisa, which of course leans to one side.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface points at the Leaning Tower of Pisa, but the leaning here is political or partial, not physical.
explanation.definitionFit: A partisan is biased, favouring one faction, so is figuratively inclined towards one side.

clue.text: Blunt language of slogan upset nervous conductor

indicators.note: something upset is knocked over and disordered, so these letters get rearranged

parts.note: taken as written
an axon is the fibre of a nerve cell that conducts impulses

explanation.surface: Someone shouts a slogan that offends a nervous orchestra conductor with its bad language.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Nervous conductor' wants to be a jittery musician; it is the nerve fibre.
explanation.definitionFit: Anglo-Saxon is an idiom for plain, coarse words, the short swear words of Old English origin.

clue.text: Cat hair covers Irving's coat

indicators.note: to cover something is to wrap around it, so one piece goes around the other

parts.note: a tress is a lock of hair

indicators.note: a coat is the outside layer, so only the outermost letters of the name are kept

parts.note: first and last letters of Irving

explanation.surface: A pet's hair gets all over the coat of someone called Irving.
explanation.definitionFit: A tigress is a female tiger, one of the big cats.

clue.text: Occasionally battlefield's full of English climbing it

indicators.note: a thing full of something holds it inside, so the battlefield wraps the rest

parts.note: the Somme, First World War battlefield, plus the possessive S
standard abbreviation

indicators.note: in a down entry, climbing means reading upwards, so the little word goes backwards

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: From time to time the English scramble up over the top on a muddy battlefield.
explanation.walkthrough: The Somme was the scene of a vast First World War battle in northern France in 1916.
explanation.definitionFit: Sometimes and occasionally are synonyms: both mean now and then, not always.

clue.text: New Barking riots left hole under bridge

parts.note: standard abbreviation

indicators.note: barking is slang for mad, and mad letters are disordered

parts.note: taken as written
standard abbreviation

explanation.surface: Fresh riots in Barking, a district of east London, leave a hole under a bridge.
explanation.walkthrough: Barking is also a London district, which is what the surface uses. The bridge is the bridge of the nose.
explanation.definitionFit: A nostril is an opening in the nose, sitting just below its bony bridge.

clue.text: That man breaks first commandment

indicators.note: breaking into something means getting inside it, so one word goes within the other

parts.note: first place is the best
pronoun for that man

explanation.surface: A man breaks the first of the Ten Commandments.
explanation.definitionFit: A behest is an order or command, so it can stand for a commandment.

clue.text: Bill catches large fish

indicators.note: something that catches another holds it, so one piece sits inside the other

parts.note: a bird's bill is its beak
standard abbreviation, as on clothing sizes

explanation.surface: A bird's bill snaps up a big fish.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bill' looks like a person's name; it is a beak.
explanation.definitionFit: The bleak is a small silvery European freshwater fish of the carp family.

clue.text: Smell that's iffy probed by doctor without interest

indicators.note: a probe goes into something, so the doctor is pushed inside the other letters

parts.note: hum is slang for a bad smell
um is the noise a doubtful speaker makes
standard abbreviation

explanation.surface: A doctor probes a dubious smell without much enthusiasm.
explanation.definitionFit: Humdrum means dull and monotonous, lacking anything to hold the attention.

clue.text: Ship back from Calais on purpose

indicators.note: the back of a word is its tail, so only its final letter is taken

parts.note: last letter of Calais
an end is an aim or purpose

explanation.surface: A ship heads back from the French port of Calais on purpose.
explanation.walkthrough: 'On' puts the S onto the front of END, the end being the goal one has in mind.
explanation.definitionFit: To ship goods is to send them off to a destination, so the verbs are synonyms.

clue.text: Back with girlfriend, initially excited

parts.note: years back means years ago

indicators.note: initially means at the start, so only the opening letter of the word is used

parts.note: first letter of girlfriend

explanation.surface: Someone is back with an old girlfriend and feeling thrilled at first.
explanation.definitionFit: Agog means eager and excited, impatiently waiting to see or hear something.

clue.text: Plan part of Christmas term in detail

indicators.note: only part of the following words is needed, so the letters sit inside them

parts.note: runs across Christmas, term, in and detail

explanation.surface: Someone plans the Christmas term at school in great detail.
explanation.definitionFit: To mastermind a scheme is to plan and direct it, so the verbs are synonyms.

clue.text: Mediator interrupted Republican, mad he's not up front

indicators.note: mad letters behave wildly, so the following words are rearranged

parts.note: taken as written
broke into, as one breaks off or interrupts
standard abbreviation

explanation.surface: A mediator cuts off an angry Republican who is not being upfront.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Up front' places the rearranged letters before BROKE+R; it is not an accusation of dishonesty.
explanation.definitionFit: An honest broker is a neutral go-between who negotiates fairly between two parties.

clue.text: Inconsiderate aunt exposed family in article

indicators.note: exposed means stripped of its outer covering, so the outside letters go

parts.note: aunt without its first and last letters

indicators.note: in places the family word inside the article word

parts.note: an article is an object, a thing
kin are one's family

explanation.surface: A tactless aunt exposes family secrets in a newspaper article.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Article' looks like a newspaper piece or a grammatical a/the; here it is just an object.
explanation.definitionFit: Unthinking behaviour is careless of others' feelings, which is what inconsiderate means.

clue.text: Workers having day out order a cab

indicators.note: out means gone, so that letter is dropped from the word

parts.note: hands are workers, as in farmhands
standard abbreviation
the Order of Merit, a British honour

explanation.surface: Workers on a day out phone to order a cab home.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Order a cab' reads as one action, but 'order' is OM and only 'a cab' defines.
explanation.definitionFit: A hansom is a two-wheeled horse-drawn cab of Victorian London, driven from a seat at the back.

clue.text: Play wearing medical dressing that's really strong tissue

indicators.note: the thing worn surrounds the wearer, so one word wraps the other

parts.note: lint is soft fabric used for dressing wounds
a game is play

explanation.surface: A child at play wears a bandage that is made of really tough material.
explanation.definitionFit: A ligament is a band of tough fibrous connective tissue binding bones together.

clue.text: Song recalling Texas girl with underwear on

parts.note: gal is informal for a girl
in Britain a vest is an undershirt
taken as written

explanation.surface: A song brings back memories of a Texan girl dressed only in her underwear.
explanation.walkthrough: In British English a vest is worn under a shirt, not over it as in American usage.
explanation.definitionFit: Galveston, a 1969 hit for Glen Campbell, is named after the Texas port city it remembers.

clue.text: Dodgy coins ref used for evidence in court

indicators.note: dodgy means unreliable or crooked, so the letters are not straight and get rearranged

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A referee's counterfeit coins are produced as evidence at his trial.
explanation.definitionFit: Forensic comes from the Latin for the forum, and describes science or methods applied in courts of law.

clue.text: Back last runner at 'aydock?

indicators.note: the dropped aitch in the racecourse name says local speech drops the same letter here

parts.note: the last part is the end
a racehorse is a runner

explanation.surface: A punter backs the horse running last at Haydock races.
explanation.walkthrough: Haydock Park is a racecourse in north-west England; writing it 'aydock tells you the runner loses its H.
explanation.definitionFit: To endorse a candidate is to support or back them publicly.

clue.text: Lean brainbox who collaborated with Watson heard from Spooner, with mystery

indicators.note: Reverend Spooner swapped the opening sounds of words, so the first sounds are exchanged

parts.note: Francis Crick, who with James Watson found the structure of DNA; he takes the opening sound of the other word
to lean is to tip; it takes the opening sound of the scientist's name

explanation.surface: A thin genius who worked with Watson is heard talking, mysteriously.
explanation.walkthrough: Swap the first sounds of TIP CRICK to hear 'crip tick'. 'Lean' looks like the adjective thin; it is the verb.
explanation.definitionFit: Cryptic means having a hidden or puzzling meaning, so it is full of mystery.

clue.text: Hate word in clue that requires alternate letters to be removed

indicators.note: in tells us the promise word sits inside the other letters

indicators.text: that requires alternate letters to be removed
indicators.note: removing every other letter keeps only the even-numbered letters of the word before

parts.note: second and fourth letters of clue
giving your word is swearing an oath

explanation.surface: A solver complains about the clues they hate most: ones that make you strip out every other letter.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue reads like a grumble about a clue type, but 'clue' is the fodder and 'word' is a promise.
explanation.definitionFit: To loathe is to feel intense dislike or disgust for something, a strong synonym for hate.

clue.text: Like a neck twisted sideways

parts.note: as means like

indicators.note: twisted means bent out of shape, so the letters lose their order

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone with a twisted neck can only look sideways.
explanation.definitionFit: Askance means with a sidelong glance, looking out of the corner of the eye, often with suspicion.

clue.text: New trike Eddy bust in two f****** days

indicators.note: something bust is broken, so its letters are smashed and remade

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Eddy breaks his new tricycle and spends two days swearing about it.
explanation.walkthrough: The asterisks look like a censored swearword, but they hide a cheekier meaning: a weekend away for sex.
explanation.definitionFit: A dirty weekend is a British idiom for a two-day romantic getaway spent mainly in bed.

clue.text: Place to sleep, temperature requiring jumpers on

parts.note: roos, short for kangaroos, are jumpers
standard abbreviation

explanation.surface: To get to sleep in a cold room you need to put your jumpers on.
explanation.walkthrough: A jumper is a British sweater, which is what the surface means; in the down entry 'on' puts ROOS above T.
explanation.definitionFit: A roost is where birds settle to sleep, and loosely any resting place.

clue.text: Body part Henry trapped in vice

indicators.note: trapped in means caught inside, so one letter sits within the other word

parts.note: a vice is a sin
the henry is the unit of inductance, symbol H

explanation.surface: A man named Henry has a body part caught in a workshop vice.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Vice' suggests the clamp; it is wickedness.
explanation.definitionFit: The shin is the front of the leg below the knee, a part of the body.

clue.text: Automatic control which bags queen the largest share

indicators.note: to bag is to put into a bag, so one word holds the others inside

parts.note: which and that are both relative pronouns
Elizabeth Regina
the most is the largest share

explanation.surface: A device that grabs the biggest portion for the queen.
explanation.definitionFit: A thermostat regulates temperature automatically by switching heating or cooling on and off.

clue.text: 50% of brides-to-be flipping innocent

indicators.note: flipping something turns it over, so the kept letters run the other way
half the word is kept and the other half thrown away

parts.note: women engaged to be married

explanation.surface: Half of the engaged women are innocents, which is flipping amazing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Flipping' poses as a mild British swear word; it is the turnaround signal.
explanation.definitionFit: Naif, from the French, describes someone naive and unworldly, or such a person.

clue.text: Eat for a laugh when talking

indicators.note: talking means speech, so the phrase is judged by how it is said

parts.note: said in jest is said for a laugh

explanation.surface: Someone eats something just for a laugh while chatting.
explanation.definitionFit: To ingest is to take food into the body by swallowing, which is what eating does.

clue.text: Meet Charlie by the side of the road

parts.note: Charlie is C in the NATO alphabet

parts.words: by the side of the road
parts.note: on the verge, a verge being the grass strip beside a British road

explanation.surface: Arrange to meet Charlie at the roadside.
explanation.definitionFit: Lines or people that converge come together at one point, so they meet.
